issues.quote: It was very weak and could not stand. Nobody wanted the horse. So Billy took it home.
issues.problem: A boy alone taking home a horse that cannot stand is a contradiction the reader notices; no other level says the horse could not stand (B1+ say it was lying down and was pushed and pulled home).
issues.fix: It was very thin and weak. Nobody wanted the horse. So Billy took it home.

notes: Fidelity: in the novel the eldest son Jim is part of the family story (he works and dies that winter). A1 omits him, which is acceptable condensing.
'Good things come in the end' is a light idiom but understandable from context; 'Good things come at last' is an alternative if needed.
'Her husband died many years before.' reads slightly odd without past perfect; 'Her husband was dead.' or 'Her husband died many years ago.' is more natural within A2 grammar.

Fidelity: 'Her oldest child worked far away in another town.' replaces the novel's eldest son Jim, who works locally and dies early in the book. Softening is allowed, but simply omitting the eldest child would be more faithful than inventing a new situation (applies to all levels).

Perfect tenses are allowed at B1, so the past-perfect avoidance sounds stilted in places: 'Her husband died years before' -> 'Her husband had died years before'; 'It was the first time any of them saw a real theater' -> 'had seen'; 'He heard about the Wiggs family' -> 'He had heard'.
'Her oldest boy was working far away in another town.' - see Jim note under A2.

issues.quote: Billy asked whether he could take it, and the man shrugged and said the animal was his.
issues.problem: 'his' most naturally reads as the owner claiming the horse is still his own, which contradicts him giving it away; the intended meaning (it is Billy's now) is unclear.
issues.fix: Billy asked whether he could take it, and the man shrugged and said he could have it.

notes: 'She was in love with a young man, and he had loved her too' suggests he no longer loves her, which slightly undercuts the reconciliation; 'and he loved her too' is clearer.
'Her oldest boy had gone to work in another town.' - see Jim note under A2.

'Out of the basket came a whole Christmas dinner, followed by bread, oranges, a frosted cake and a box of candy.' - bread and cake read as part of a whole dinner; consider 'a whole Christmas dinner, with oranges, a frosted cake and a box of candy besides.'
'a young man who had loved her in return' -> 'who loved her in return' avoids implying the love is over.
The eldest boy 'sending home what he could' replaces Jim's story; see note under A2.
The closing line closely and pleasingly echoes the novel's famous last line.

summary: A faithful, gentle and age-appropriate condensation with correct quizzes and level-appropriate language at every level. Two small concrete fixes are needed: the A1 horse that 'could not stand' yet is taken home, and the ambiguous B2 sentence where the owner 'said the animal was his'. The eldest son Jim is replaced by a boy working away from home, which is noted as softening rather than failed.
